P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

AB is a tangent at B to a circle with centre O, and A is a point outside the circle with ∠AOB=52°\angle AOB = 52°∠AOB=52°. Then ∠OAB\angle OAB∠OAB is:

Theorem 10.1 — the right angle is at the point of contact B (Topic 3). Why it applies: OB is the radius to the point of contact.

That is the angle at O, not at A.
The two acute angles of right △OBA add up to 90°.
The right angle is at B, not at the outside point A.
180°−52°180° - 52°180°−52° forgets the right angle.

Given: AB touches the circle at B; ∠AOB=52°\angle AOB = 52°∠AOB=52°. Asked: ∠OAB\angle OAB∠OAB.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 — the right angle is at the point of contact B (Topic 3). Why it applies: OB is the radius to the point of contact.

  1. 1

    ∠OBA=90°\angle OBA = 90°∠OBA=90° (tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact).

  2. 2

    In △OAB: ∠OAB=180°−90°−52°=38°\angle OAB = 180° - 90° - 52° = 38°∠OAB=180°−90°−52°=38°.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔ The two acute angles of right △OBA add up to 90°.
    • (a) ✘ That is the angle at O, not at A.
    • (c) ✘ The right angle is at B, not at the outside point A.
    • (d) ✘ 180°−52°180° - 52°180°−52° forgets the right angle.

  3. Check: 38°+52°+90°=180°38° + 52° + 90° = 180°38°+52°+90°=180° ✔.

  4. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Putting the right angle at A because "the tangent starts at A". The right angle is always where the tangent touches the circle.
P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A point P is 20 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 16 cm. The length of the tangent from P is:

Theorem 10.1 and Pythagoras with OP as the hypotenuse (Topic 3). Why it applies: the right angle is at T.

20−1620 - 1620−16 subtracts lengths, not squares.
202−162=12\sqrt{20^2 - 16^2} = 12202−162​=12.
202+162=656=441\sqrt{20^2 + 16^2} = \sqrt{656} = 4\sqrt{41}202+162​=656​=441​ treats OP as a shorter side.
20+1620 + 1620+16 adds the lengths.

Given: OP=20OP = 20OP=20 cm; r=16r = 16r=16 cm. Asked: PT.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 and Pythagoras with OP as the hypotenuse (Topic 3). Why it applies: the right angle is at T.

  1. 1

    ∠OTP=90°\angle OTP = 90°∠OTP=90° (tangent ⟂ radius), so PT2=OP2−OT2=400−256=144PT^2 = OP^2 - OT^2 = 400 - 256 = 144PT2=OP2−OT2=400−256=144.

  2. 2

    PT=12PT = 12PT=12 cm.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔ 202−162=12\sqrt{20^2 - 16^2} = 12202−162​=12.
    • (a) ✘ 20−1620 - 1620−16 subtracts lengths, not squares.
    • (c) ✘ 202+162=656=441\sqrt{20^2 + 16^2} = \sqrt{656} = 4\sqrt{41}202+162​=656​=441​ treats OP as a shorter side.
    • (d) ✘ 20+1620 + 1620+16 adds the lengths.

  3. Check: 122+162=144+256=400=20212^2 + 16^2 = 144 + 256 = 400 = 20^2122+162=144+256=400=202 ✔.

  4. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Choosing (c): the tangent is never longer than OP, because OP is the hypotenuse.

PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and ∠AOB=140°\angle AOB = 140°∠AOB=140°. Then ∠APB\angle APB∠APB is:

the kite OAPB: ∠APB+∠AOB=180°\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°∠APB+∠AOB=180° (Topic 4). Why it applies: the angles at A and B are right angles.

The two angles are not equal.
Halving 140° gives ∠AOP\angle AOP∠AOP, not ∠APB\angle APB∠APB.
Supplementary to 140°.
This is ∠OPA\angle OPA∠OPA, half of ∠APB\angle APB∠APB.

Given: ∠AOB=140°\angle AOB = 140°∠AOB=140°. Asked: ∠APB\angle APB∠APB.

Concept used: the kite OAPB: ∠APB+∠AOB=180°\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°∠APB+∠AOB=180° (Topic 4). Why it applies: the angles at A and B are right angles.

  1. 1

    ∠OAP=∠OBP=90°\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90°∠OAP=∠OBP=90° (tangent ⟂ radius).

  2. 2

    ∠APB=360°−90°−90°−140°=40°\angle APB = 360° - 90° - 90° - 140° = 40°∠APB=360°−90°−90°−140°=40°.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (c) ✔ Supplementary to 140°.
    • (a) ✘ The two angles are not equal.
    • (b) ✘ Halving 140° gives ∠AOP\angle AOP∠AOP, not ∠APB\angle APB∠APB.
    • (d) ✘ This is ∠OPA\angle OPA∠OPA, half of ∠APB\angle APB∠APB.

  3. Check: 40°+140°=180°40° + 140° = 180°40°+140°=180° ✔.

P4● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A point is 4 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. The number of tangents to the circle through this point is:

inside → 0; on → 1; outside → 2 (Topic 2). Why it applies: 4<64 < 64<6, so the point is inside.

Given: distance 4 cm; radius 6 cm. Asked: the number of tangents.

Concept used: inside → 0; on → 1; outside → 2 (Topic 2). Why it applies: 4<64 < 64<6, so the point is inside.

  1. 1

    4<64 < 64<6: the point is inside the circle.

  2. 2

    Every line through it cuts the circle twice, so no tangent passes through it.

    Reasoning for each option: (a) ✔. (b) is for a point on the circle; (c) for a point outside; (d) is the number of tangents the circle has altogether.

  3. Check: a line through an inside point goes out of the circle on both sides — two common points ✔.

  4. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Answering (c) out of habit — "two tangents from a point" is true only for a point outside.
P5● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markOriginal

Write True or False and justify: "From a point outside a circle, exactly one tangent can be drawn to the circle."

Full solution

Given: a point outside a circle. Asked: true or false.

Concept used: the counting facts (Topic 2). Why it applies: the point is outside.

  1. 1

    From a point outside a circle there are exactly two tangents, one on each side of the line to the centre.

  2. Check: draw a circle and mark a point outside it; a ruler through the point can be turned until it just touches the circle on the left, and again on the right — two positions ✔.

  3. Answer False — exactly two tangents can be drawn from a point outside a circle.

    Common trap: Mixing up "on" and "outside": exactly one tangent passes through a point on the circle.

P6● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Two concentric circles have radii 37 cm and 12 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle that touches the smaller circle.

Full solution

Given: radii 37 cm and 12 cm. Asked: the chord AB, touching the small circle at M.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 (OM⊥ABOM \perp ABOM⊥AB); the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord; Pythagoras (Topic 3). Why it applies: AB is a tangent of the small circle and a chord of the big one.

  1. 1

    OM⊥ABOM \perp ABOM⊥AB (tangent ⟂ radius at M), so M is the mid-point of AB.

  2. 2

    MB=372−122=1369−144=1225=35MB = \sqrt{37^2 - 12^2} = \sqrt{1369 - 144} = \sqrt{1225} = 35MB=372−122​=1369−144​=1225​=35 cm.

  3. 3

    AB=2×35=70AB = 2 \times 35 = 70AB=2×35=70 cm.

  4. Check: 122+352=144+1225=1369=37212^2 + 35^2 = 144 + 1225 = 1369 = 37^2122+352=144+1225=1369=372 ✔.

  5. Answer 70 cm

    Common trap: Answering 35 cm — only half the chord.

P7● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle. AB=6AB = 6AB=6 cm, BC=7BC = 7BC=7 cm and CD=9CD = 9CD=9 cm. Then AD is:

AB+CD=AD+BCAB + CD = AD + BCAB+CD=AD+BC (Topic 5). Why it applies: every side is a tangent.

AB+BC−CD=4AB + BC - CD = 4AB+BC−CD=4 pairs adjacent sides.
Opposite sides have equal sums.
BC+CD−AB=10BC + CD - AB = 10BC+CD−AB=10 also pairs adjacent sides.
This adds the three given sides.

Given: three sides of a circumscribed quadrilateral. Asked: AD.

Concept used: AB+CD=AD+BCAB + CD = AD + BCAB+CD=AD+BC (Topic 5). Why it applies: every side is a tangent.

  1. 1

    6+9=AD+76 + 9 = AD + 76+9=AD+7, so AD=8AD = 8AD=8 cm.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (b) ✔ Opposite sides have equal sums.
    • (a) ✘ AB+BC−CD=4AB + BC - CD = 4AB+BC−CD=4 pairs adjacent sides.
    • (c) ✘ BC+CD−AB=10BC + CD - AB = 10BC+CD−AB=10 also pairs adjacent sides.
    • (d) ✘ This adds the three given sides.

  2. Check: tangent pieces 2, 4, 3 and 6 cm from A, B, C and D give sides 6, 7, 9 and 8 ✔.

  3. Answer (b)

    Common trap: Writing AB+BC=CD+DAAB + BC = CD + DAAB+BC=CD+DA — the sums are of opposite sides.
P8● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Kabir wrote this proof that the tangents PQ and PR from P to a circle with centre O are equal. Find his mistake and correct it.
"Join OQ, OR, OP. In △OQP and △ORP: OQ = OR (radii); OP = OP (common); ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90°. So △OQP ≅ △ORP by SAS, and PQ = PR."

Full solution

Given: Kabir's proof. Asked: the mistake and the correction.

Concept used: SAS needs the angle between the two sides; RHS needs right angles, the hypotenuse and one side (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: the right angles are at Q and R.

  1. 1

    In △OQP, the angle between OQ and OP is ∠QOP\angle QOP∠QOP, not ∠OQP\angle OQP∠OQP. The right angle is not between the two equal sides, so SAS does not apply.

  2. 2

    The triangles are right-angled at Q and R, OP is the hypotenuse of both, and OQ = OR — this is exactly RHS.

  3. 3

    Also, "∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90°" needs its reason: tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact.

  4. Check: the corrected proof has five lines, each with a reason — as in the Topic 4 table ✔.

  5. Answer The rule should be RHS, not SAS (the right angle is not between OQ and OP), and the right angles need the reason "tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact".

    Common trap: Thinking any three equal parts make SAS. The angle must be the one between the two sides.

P9● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

PA is a tangent from P to a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm, and ∠OPA=45°\angle OPA = 45°∠OPA=45°. Find PA and OP.

Full solution

Given: r=6r = 6r=6 cm; ∠OPA=45°\angle OPA = 45°∠OPA=45°. Asked: PA and OP.

Concept used: right △OAP (Theorem 10.1); tan and sin of 45° (Topic 4). Why it applies: we know the radius and an angle.

  1. 1

    ∠OAP=90°\angle OAP = 90°∠OAP=90° (tangent ⟂ radius). tan⁡45°=OAPA\tan 45° = \dfrac{OA}{PA}tan45°=PAOA​, so 1=6PA1 = \dfrac{6}{PA}1=PA6​ and PA=6PA = 6PA=6 cm.

  2. 2

    sin⁡45°=OAOP\sin 45° = \dfrac{OA}{OP}sin45°=OPOA​, so 12=6OP\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{6}{OP}2​1​=OP6​ and OP=62OP = 6\sqrt{2}OP=62​ cm.

  3. Check: 62+62=72=(62)26^2 + 6^2 = 72 = (6\sqrt{2})^262+62=72=(62​)2 ✔.

  4. Answer PA=6PA = 6PA=6 cm; OP=62OP = 6\sqrt{2}OP=62​ cm (about 8.49 cm)

    Common trap: Using sin⁡45°\sin 45°sin45° for PA. PA is next to the 45° angle, and the radius is opposite it — that pair goes with tan.

P10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

AT is the tangent at A to a circle with centre O, and AB is a chord. The angle between the chord and the tangent, ∠BAT\angle BAT∠BAT, is 62°. Find ∠AOB\angle AOB∠AOB.

Full solution

Given: ∠BAT=62°\angle BAT = 62°∠BAT=62°. Asked: ∠AOB\angle AOB∠AOB.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 (∠OAT=90°\angle OAT = 90°∠OAT=90°); equal radii make △OAB isosceles (Topics 1, 3). Why it applies: OA is the radius to the point of contact.

  1. 1

    ∠OAT=90°\angle OAT = 90°∠OAT=90° (tangent ⟂ radius), so ∠OAB=90°−62°=28°\angle OAB = 90° - 62° = 28°∠OAB=90°−62°=28°.

  2. 2

    OA=OBOA = OBOA=OB (radii), so ∠OBA=28°\angle OBA = 28°∠OBA=28°.

  3. 3

    ∠AOB=180°−28°−28°=124°\angle AOB = 180° - 28° - 28° = 124°∠AOB=180°−28°−28°=124°.

  4. Check: ∠AOB=2×62°=124°\angle AOB = 2 \times 62° = 124°∠AOB=2×62°=124° — the angle at the centre is twice the angle between the tangent and the chord ✔ (Practice question 25 proves this).

  5. Answer 124°

    Common trap: Putting the right angle between the chord and the tangent. The right angle is between the radius OA and the tangent.

Full solution

Given: r=28r = 28r=28 cm; PT=45PT = 45PT=45 cm. Asked: OP.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 and Pythagoras: OP is the hypotenuse (Topic 3). Why it applies: the right angle is at T.

    OP2=OT2+PT2=282+452=784+2025=2809OP^2 = OT^2 + PT^2 = 28^2 + 45^2 = 784 + 2025 = 2809OP2=OT2+PT2=282+452=784+2025=2809.

    OP=2809=53OP = \sqrt{2809} = 53OP=2809​=53 cm.

  3. Check: 53>4553 > 4553>45 and 53>2853 > 2853>28 — the hypotenuse is the longest side ✔.

  4. Answer 53 cm

    Common trap: 452−282=1241\sqrt{45^2 - 28^2} = \sqrt{1241}452−282​=1241​: here OP is the side to find, and it is the hypotenuse — add the squares.

P12●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O, and ∠AOB\angle AOB∠AOB is twice ∠APB\angle APB∠APB. Find both angles.

Full solution

Given: ∠AOB=2∠APB\angle AOB = 2\angle APB∠AOB=2∠APB. Asked: both angles.

Concept used: ∠APB+∠AOB=180°\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°∠APB+∠AOB=180° (Topic 4). Why it applies: OAPB has right angles at A and B.

  1. 1

    Let ∠APB=x\angle APB = x∠APB=x. Then ∠AOB=2x\angle AOB = 2x∠AOB=2x.

    x+2x=180°x + 2x = 180°x+2x=180°, so 3x=180°3x = 180°3x=180° and x=60°x = 60°x=60°.

    ∠APB=60°\angle APB = 60°∠APB=60°, ∠AOB=120°\angle AOB = 120°∠AOB=120°.

  4. Check: 60°+120°=180°60° + 120° = 180°60°+120°=180° ✔, and 120°=2×60°120° = 2 \times 60°120°=2×60° ✔.

  5. Answer ∠APB=60°\angle APB = 60°∠APB=60°, ∠AOB=120°\angle AOB = 120°∠AOB=120°

P13●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

In two concentric circles, a chord of the larger circle is 24 cm long and touches the smaller circle, whose radius is 9 cm. Find the radius of the larger circle.

Full solution

Given: chord AB=24AB = 24AB=24 cm touching the small circle at M; small radius OM=9OM = 9OM=9 cm. Asked: the large radius OB.

Concept used: OM⊥ABOM \perp ABOM⊥AB and M bisects AB; Pythagoras (Topic 3). Why it applies: AB is a tangent to the small circle.

  1. 1

    OM⊥ABOM \perp ABOM⊥AB (tangent ⟂ radius at M), so MB=242=12MB = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12MB=224​=12 cm.

  2. 2

    OB=OM2+MB2=81+144=225=15OB = \sqrt{OM^2 + MB^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15OB=OM2+MB2​=81+144​=225​=15 cm.

  3. Check: 92+122=225=1529^2 + 12^2 = 225 = 15^292+122=225=152 ✔.

  4. Answer 15 cm

    Common trap: Using the whole chord: 92+242=657\sqrt{9^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{657}92+242​=657​ cm. Only half the chord is a side of triangle OMB.

P14●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A circle is inscribed in △ABC, touching AB at F, BC at D and CA at E. AB=11AB = 11AB=11 cm, BC=15BC = 15BC=15 cm and CA=12CA = 12CA=12 cm. Find AF, BD and CE.

Full solution

Given: the three sides. Asked: the tangent pieces at A, B and C.

Concept used: equal tangent pieces; piece at a corner =s−= s -=s− the opposite side (Topic 5). Why it applies: each corner is an external point.

  1. 1

    Let AF=AE=xAF = AE = xAF=AE=x, BF=BD=yBF = BD = yBF=BD=y, CD=CE=zCD = CE = zCD=CE=z (tangents from an external point are equal).

  2. 2

    s=11+15+122=19s = \dfrac{11 + 15 + 12}{2} = 19s=211+15+12​=19 cm.

  3. 3

    x=s−BC=4x = s - BC = 4x=s−BC=4 cm; y=s−CA=7y = s - CA = 7y=s−CA=7 cm; z=s−AB=8z = s - AB = 8z=s−AB=8 cm.

  4. Check: 4+7=114 + 7 = 114+7=11, 7+8=157 + 8 = 157+8=15, 8+4=128 + 4 = 128+4=12 ✔.

  5. Answer AF=4AF = 4AF=4 cm, BD=7BD = 7BD=7 cm, CE=8CE = 8CE=8 cm

    Common trap: Setting AF=BDAF = BDAF=BD because "tangents are equal". AF and BD start from different corners — only the two pieces from the same corner are equal.

P15●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Two tangents PA and PB to a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm are inclined to each other at 120°. Find PA and OP.

Full solution

Given: ∠APB=120°\angle APB = 120°∠APB=120°; r=6r = 6r=6 cm. Asked: PA and OP.

Concept used: OP bisects ∠APB\angle APB∠APB; right △OAP; tan and sin of 60° (Topic 4). Why it applies: we know the radius and an angle.

    ∠OPA=120°2=60°\angle OPA = \dfrac{120°}{2} = 60°∠OPA=2120°​=60° (OP bisects the angle between the tangents); ∠OAP=90°\angle OAP = 90°∠OAP=90°.

  2. 2

    tan⁡60°=OAPA\tan 60° = \dfrac{OA}{PA}tan60°=PAOA​: 3=6PA\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{6}{PA}3​=PA6​, so PA=63=23PA = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3}PA=3​6​=23​ cm.

  3. 3

    sin⁡60°=OAOP\sin 60° = \dfrac{OA}{OP}sin60°=OPOA​: 32=6OP\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{6}{OP}23​​=OP6​, so OP=123=43OP = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{3}} = 4\sqrt{3}OP=3​12​=43​ cm.

P16●● StandardProof · 3 marksOriginal

PA and PB are tangents from P to a circle with centre O. Q is any point on the segment OP. Prove that QA=QBQA = QBQA=QB.

Full solution

Given: tangents PA, PB; Q on OP. To prove: QA=QBQA = QBQA=QB.

Concept used: Theorem 10.2 (PA=PBPA = PBPA=PB) and the bisected angle at P; SAS (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: triangles PQA and PQB have two pairs of equal sides and the angle between them equal.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. PA=PBPA = PBPA=PB Tangents from an external point are equal
    2. ∠APQ=∠BPQ\angle APQ = \angle BPQ∠APQ=∠BPQ OP bisects the angle between the tangents (△OAP ≅ △OBP by RHS; CPCT); Q is on OP
    3. PQ=PQPQ = PQPQ=PQ Common
    4. △PQA≅△PQB\triangle PQA \cong \triangle PQB△PQA≅△PQB SAS (the equal angles are between the equal sides)
    5. QA=QBQA = QBQA=QB CPCT. Hence proved.

  2. Check (with numbers): radius 6, OP=10OP = 10OP=10, Q the mid-point of OP: A and B are at (3.6,±4.8)(3.6, \pm 4.8)(3.6,±4.8) and Q at (5,0)(5, 0)(5,0), so QA=QB=1.42+4.82=5QA = QB = \sqrt{1.4^2 + 4.8^2} = 5QA=QB=1.42+4.82​=5 ✔.

  3. Answer QA=QBQA = QBQA=QB — proved.

    Common trap: Leaving out the reason for step 2. "OP bisects ∠APB" is itself a result; quote where it comes from.

P17●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

PQ is a chord of a circle with centre O, and PR is the tangent at P. The tangent makes an angle of 58° with the chord: ∠QPR=58°\angle QPR = 58°∠QPR=58°. Then ∠POQ\angle POQ∠POQ is:

∠OPR=90°\angle OPR = 90°∠OPR=90° (Theorem 10.1); isosceles △OPQ (Topic 3). Why it applies: OP is the radius to the point of contact.

This copies the tangent–chord angle.
This is ∠OPQ\angle OPQ∠OPQ.
This is ∠OPQ+∠OQP\angle OPQ + \angle OQP∠OPQ+∠OQP, not the angle at O.
180°−2×32°180° - 2 \times 32°180°−2×32°.

    ∠OPQ=90°−58°=32°\angle OPQ = 90° - 58° = 32°∠OPQ=90°−58°=32°.

    OP=OQOP = OQOP=OQ, so ∠OQP=32°\angle OQP = 32°∠OQP=32°, and ∠POQ=180°−64°=116°\angle POQ = 180° - 64° = 116°∠POQ=180°−64°=116°.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (d) ✔ 180°−2×32°180° - 2 \times 32°180°−2×32°.
    • (a) ✘ This copies the tangent–chord angle.

    Half-chord =52−42=3= \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3=52−42​=3 cm, so the chord is 6 cm.

    Common trap: Choosing (A), half the chord.

E12●● StandardProof · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.3 Q2

Two tangents PQ and PR are drawn from an external point to a circle with centre O. Prove that QORP is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Full solution

Given: tangents PQ and PR. To prove: QORP is cyclic.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1; a quadrilateral whose opposite angles add up to 180° is cyclic (Class 9). Why it applies: the angles at Q and R are right angles.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. ∠OQP=∠ORP=90°\angle OQP = \angle ORP = 90°∠OQP=∠ORP=90° Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact
    2. ∠OQP+∠ORP=180°\angle OQP + \angle ORP = 180°∠OQP+∠ORP=180° Step 1; these are opposite angles of QORP
    3. QORP is cyclic A quadrilateral with a pair of opposite angles adding up to 180° is cyclic (Class 9). Hence proved.

  2. Check: then also ∠QOR+∠QPR=180°\angle QOR + \angle QPR = 180°∠QOR+∠QPR=180°, which is NCERT Exercise 10.2 Q10 ✔.

  3. Answer QORP is cyclic — proved.

    Common trap: Forgetting to say that Q and R are opposite vertices of QORP.

You got 0 of 1 parts.

Given: tangents BC, BD; ∠DBC=120°\angle DBC = 120°∠DBC=120°. To prove: BO=2BCBO = 2BCBO=2BC.

Concept used: OB bisects the angle; cos 60° (Topic 4). Why it applies: △OCB is right-angled at C.

    1. ∠OBC=60°\angle OBC = 60°∠OBC=60° OB bisects ∠DBC\angle DBC∠DBC (△OCB ≅ △ODB by RHS; CPCT)
    2. ∠OCB=90°\angle OCB = 90°∠OCB=90° Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact
    3. cos⁡60°=BCBO\cos 60° = \dfrac{BC}{BO}cos60°=BOBC​, so BO=2BCBO = 2BCBO=2BC Right △OCB; cos⁡60°=12\cos 60° = \dfrac{1}{2}cos60°=21​
    4. BC+BD=2BC=BOBC + BD = 2BC = BOBC+BD=2BC=BO BD=BCBD = BCBD=BC (tangents from B). Hence proved.

E14●●● AdvancedProof · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.3 Q5

In Fig. 9.13, AB and CD are common tangents to two circles of unequal radii. Prove that AB = CD.

(Fig. 9.13, described: a large circle on the left and a small circle on the right, not meeting; the line AB touches the large circle at A (top) and the small one at B; the line CD touches the large circle at C (bottom) and the small one at D. Both lines pass above and below the circles, and they slope towards each other on the right.)

Full solution

Given: AB and CD touch both circles; the radii are unequal. To prove: AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD. Construction: extend AB and CD to meet at P (they meet on the side of the smaller circle, because the radii are unequal).

Concept used: Theorem 10.2 for each circle from the same point P (Topic 5). Why it applies: P is outside both circles.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. PA=PCPA = PCPA=PC Tangents from P to the large circle
    2. PB=PDPB = PDPB=PD Tangents from P to the small circle
    3. PA−PB=PC−PDPA - PB = PC - PDPA−PB=PC−PD Subtract step 2 from step 1
    4. AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD B lies between P and A, and D between P and C. Hence proved.

  2. Check (with numbers): if the tangents from P are 12 cm to the large circle and 4 cm to the small one, then AB=CD=12−4=8AB = CD = 12 - 4 = 8AB=CD=12−4=8 cm ✔.

  3. Answer AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD — proved.

    Common trap: Trying to use the radii — they are unequal and not needed.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

E15●● StandardProof · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.3 Q7

In Fig. 9.14, common tangents AB and CD to two circles intersect at E. Prove that AB = CD.

(Fig. 9.14, described: two separate circles; AB touches the left circle at A and the right circle at B; CD touches the left circle at C and the right circle at D; AB and CD cross at E between the circles.)

Full solution

Given: AB and CD touch both circles and cross at E. To prove: AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD.

Concept used: Theorem 10.2 at E for each circle (Topic 5). Why it applies: E is outside both circles.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. EA=ECEA = ECEA=EC Tangents from E to the left circle
    2. EB=EDEB = EDEB=ED Tangents from E to the right circle
    3. EA+EB=EC+EDEA + EB = EC + EDEA+EB=EC+ED Add steps 1 and 2
    4. AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD E lies between A and B and between C and D. Hence proved.

  2. Check: if EA=5EA = 5EA=5 and EB=3EB = 3EB=3, then AB=CD=8AB = CD = 8AB=CD=8 ✔.

  3. Answer AB=CDAB = CDAB=CD — proved.

    Common trap: Writing EA=EBEA = EBEA=EB: those are tangents to different circles.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

E16●● StandardProof · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.4 Q1

If a hexagon ABCDEF circumscribe a circle, prove that AB + CD + EF = BC + DE + FA.

Full solution

Given: ABCDEF circumscribes a circle. To prove: AB+CD+EF=BC+DE+FAAB + CD + EF = BC + DE + FAAB+CD+EF=BC+DE+FA.

Concept used: equal tangent pieces at each corner (Topic 5). Why it applies: every corner is an external point.

  1. 1

    Let the tangent pieces at A, B, C, D, E, F be a,b,c,d,e,fa, b, c, d, e, fa,b,c,d,e,f (tangents from an external point are equal).

  2. 2

    AB+CD+EF=(a+b)+(c+d)+(e+f)AB + CD + EF = (a + b) + (c + d) + (e + f)AB+CD+EF=(a+b)+(c+d)+(e+f).

  3. 3

    BC+DE+FA=(b+c)+(d+e)+(f+a)BC + DE + FA = (b + c) + (d + e) + (f + a)BC+DE+FA=(b+c)+(d+e)+(f+a).

  4. 4

    Both equal a+b+c+d+e+fa + b + c + d + e + fa+b+c+d+e+f. Hence proved.

  5. Check: a regular hexagon round a circle has six equal sides — both sums are three sides ✔.

  6. Answer proved.

    Common trap: Taking all six sides equal — that is true only for a regular hexagon.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

E17●● StandardProof · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.4 Q2

Let s denote the semi-perimeter of a triangle ABC in which BC = a, CA = b, AB = c. If a circle touches the sides BC, CA, AB at D, E, F, respectively, prove that BD = s – b.

Full solution

Given: the incircle touches BC, CA, AB at D, E, F. To prove: BD=s−bBD = s - bBD=s−b.

Concept used: equal tangent pieces (Topic 5). Why it applies: A, B, C are external points.

  1. 1

    AE=AF=xAE = AF = xAE=AF=x, BD=BF=yBD = BF = yBD=BF=y, CD=CE=zCD = CE = zCD=CE=z (tangents from an external point).

  2. 2

    2s=a+b+c=(y+z)+(z+x)+(x+y)=2(x+y+z)2s = a + b + c = (y + z) + (z + x) + (x + y) = 2(x + y + z)2s=a+b+c=(y+z)+(z+x)+(x+y)=2(x+y+z), so s=x+y+zs = x + y + zs=x+y+z.

  3. 3

    b=CA=z+xb = CA = z + xb=CA=z+x, so s−b=y=BDs - b = y = BDs−b=y=BD. Hence proved.

  4. Check: Topic 5, Worked example 3: s=18s = 18s=18, CA=12CA = 12CA=12, BD=6=18−12BD = 6 = 18 - 12BD=6=18−12 ✔.

  5. Answer BD=s−bBD = s - bBD=s−b — proved.

    Common trap: Writing BD=s−aBD = s - aBD=s−a — the side to subtract is the one opposite B.

    Perimeter =PC+CE+ED+DP=(PC+CA)+(DB+DP)=PA+PB=10+10=20= PC + CE + ED + DP = (PC + CA) + (DB + DP) = PA + PB = 10 + 10 = 20=PC+CE+ED+DP=(PC+CA)+(DB+DP)=PA+PB=10+10=20 cm.

E21● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.2 Q1

Write 'True' or 'False' and justify your answer: If a chord AB subtends an angle of 60° at the centre of a circle, then angle between the tangents at A and B is also 60°.

Full solution

Given: ∠AOB=60°\angle AOB = 60°∠AOB=60°; the tangents at A and B meet at P. Asked: true or false.

Concept used: the kite OAPB: ∠APB+∠AOB=180°\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°∠APB+∠AOB=180° (Topic 4). Why it applies: the angles at A and B are right angles.

  1. 1

    ∠OAP=∠OBP=90°\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90°∠OAP=∠OBP=90° (tangent ⟂ radius), so ∠APB=360°−90°−90°−60°=120°\angle APB = 360° - 90° - 90° - 60° = 120°∠APB=360°−90°−90°−60°=120°.

  2. Check: 120°+60°=180°120° + 60° = 180°120°+60°=180° ✔.

  3. Answer False — the angle between the tangents is 120°.

    Common trap: Thinking the two angles are equal. They are supplementary.

E22●● StandardProof · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.3 Q4

Prove that the centre of a circle touching two intersecting lines lies on the angle bisector of the lines.

Full solution

Given: lines ℓ\ellℓ and mmm meet at P; a circle with centre O touches ℓ\ellℓ at A and mmm at B. To prove: OP bisects ∠APB\angle APB∠APB. Construction: join OA, OB and OP.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1 and RHS — the same steps as the proof of Theorem 10.2 (Topic 4). Why it applies: PA and PB are the two tangents from P.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. ∠OAP=∠OBP=90°\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90°∠OAP=∠OBP=90° Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact
    2. OA=OBOA = OBOA=OB Radii of the same circle
    3. OP=OPOP = OPOP=OP Common
    4. △OAP≅△OBP\triangle OAP \cong \triangle OBP△OAP≅△OBP RHS
    5. ∠OPA=∠OPB\angle OPA = \angle OPB∠OPA=∠OPB, so O lies on the bisector of ∠APB\angle APB∠APB CPCT. Hence proved.

  2. Check (with numbers): the lines y=xy = xy=x and y=−xy = -xy=−x meet at P(0, 0); the circle with centre O(5, 0) and radius 52\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}2​5​ touches both, and O lies on the x-axis, which bisects the angle between the lines ✔.

  3. Answer The centre lies on the angle bisector — proved.

    Common trap: Writing "SAS" in step 4 — the right angles are not between the equal sides.

E23●● StandardProof · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.3 Q9

Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a chord of a circle make equal angles with the chord.

Full solution

Given: a chord AB of a circle with centre O; tangents ℓ\ellℓ at A and mmm at B; P on ℓ\ellℓ and Q on mmm, on the same side of AB as each other. To prove: ∠PAB=∠QBA\angle PAB = \angle QBA∠PAB=∠QBA. Construction: join OA and OB.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1; equal radii (Topics 1, 3). Why it applies: OA and OB are radii to the points of contact.

  1. Statement Reason
    1. ∠OAB=∠OBA\angle OAB = \angle OBA∠OAB=∠OBA OA=OBOA = OBOA=OB (radii): base angles of an isosceles triangle
    2. ∠OAP=∠OBQ=90°\angle OAP = \angle OBQ = 90°∠OAP=∠OBQ=90° Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact
    3. ∠PAB=90°−∠OAB=90°−∠OBA=∠QBA\angle PAB = 90° - \angle OAB = 90° - \angle OBA = \angle QBA∠PAB=90°−∠OAB=90°−∠OBA=∠QBA Steps 1 and 2. Hence proved.

  2. Check: if the tangents meet at T, then TA=TBTA = TBTA=TB (Theorem 10.2), so △TAB is isosceles and its base angles are equal — the same result ✔. If AB is a diameter, both angles are 90° ✔.

  3. Answer The two angles are equal — proved.

    Common trap: Assuming the tangents always meet. When AB is a diameter they are parallel; the radius proof above still works.

E24●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 9, Ex 9.4 Q11

In Fig. 9.20. O is the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, T is a point such that OT = 13 cm and OT intersects the circle at E. If AB is the tangent to the circle at E, find the length of AB.

(Fig. 9.20, described: a circle with centre O on the left; T outside to the right; the tangents TP (upper) and TQ (lower) from T; OT cuts the circle at E; the tangent at E meets TP at A and TQ at B.)

Full solution

Given: r=5r = 5r=5 cm; OT=13OT = 13OT=13 cm; AB the tangent at E, with A on TP and B on TQ. Asked: AB.

Concept used: Theorem 10.1, Pythagoras, Theorem 10.2 at A and B (Topics 3, 5). Why it applies: A and B are external points.

  1. 1

    ∠OPT=90°\angle OPT = 90°∠OPT=90°, so TP=132−52=12TP = \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = 12TP=132−52​=12 cm.

  2. 2

    TE=OT−OE=13−5=8TE = OT - OE = 13 - 5 = 8TE=OT−OE=13−5=8 cm, and ∠AET=90°\angle AET = 90°∠AET=90° (OE ⟂ AB, and O, E, T are on one line).

  3. 3

    Let AE=AP=xAE = AP = xAE=AP=x (tangents from A). Then TA=12−xTA = 12 - xTA=12−x.

  4. 4

    In right △AET: (12−x)2=x2+82(12 - x)^2 = x^2 + 8^2(12−x)2=x2+82, so 144−24x=64144 - 24x = 64144−24x=64 and x=103x = \dfrac{10}{3}x=310​ cm.

  5. 5

    In the same way BE=103BE = \dfrac{10}{3}BE=310​ cm, so AB=203AB = \dfrac{20}{3}AB=320​ cm.

  6. Check: TA=12−103=263TA = 12 - \dfrac{10}{3} = \dfrac{26}{3}TA=12−310​=326​, and (103)2+82=100+5769=6769=(263)2\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^2 + 8^2 = \dfrac{100 + 576}{9} = \dfrac{676}{9} = \left(\dfrac{26}{3}\right)^2(310​)2+82=9100+576​=9676​=(326​)2 ✔.

  7. Answer AB=203AB = \dfrac{20}{3}AB=320​ cm (about 6.67 cm)

    Common trap: Taking AE=TEAE = TEAE=TE or treating AB as part of the tangent TP. Name the two equal pieces at A (AP=AEAP = AEAP=AE) first.

C1 — Case: the Ferris wheel●● StandardCase/source-based · 4 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Circles, Case Study 1

(Picture, described: a photograph of a Ferris wheel with lines drawn on it, and beside it the figure Aarti draws — a circle with centre O; P outside it to the right; PR touches the circle at R (top right) and PQ at Q (the bottom); the angle RPQ is marked 30°; S is a point on the circle at the top left; QS, SR, OQ, OR and RQ are joined, and a right-angle mark is near Q.)

A Ferris wheel (or a big wheel in the United Kingdom) is an amusement ride consisting of a rotating upright wheel with multiple passenger-carrying components (commonly referred to as passenger cars, cabins, tubs, capsules, gondolas, or pods) attached to the rim in such a way that as the wheel turns, they are kept upright, usually by gravity.

After taking a ride in Ferris wheel, Aarti came out from the crowd and was observing her friends who were enjoying the ride . She was curious about the different angles and measures that the wheel will form. She forms the figure as given below.

  1. In the given figure find ∠ROQ

a) 60 b) 100 c) 150 d) 90

  1. Find ∠RQP

a) 75 b) 60 c) 30 d) 90

  1. Find ∠RSQ

a) 60 b) 75 c) 100 d) 30

  1. Find ∠ORP

a) 90 b) 70 c) 100 d) 60

(The bank's key: 1. c) 150, 2. a) 75, 3. b) 75, 4. a) 90 — all correct. Part 3 also needs a Class 9 fact: the angle an arc makes at the centre is twice the angle it makes at any point on the rest of the circle.)

Full solution

Given: PR and PQ are tangents; ∠RPQ=30°\angle RPQ = 30°∠RPQ=30°. Asked: four angles.

Concept used: the kite ORPQ; isosceles △PRQ; the Class 9 centre-angle fact (Topics 1, 4). Why it applies: PR and PQ are tangents from P.

  1. 1

    Part 1: ∠ROQ=180°−30°=150°\angle ROQ = 180° - 30° = 150°∠ROQ=180°−30°=150° → c).

  2. 2

    Part 2: PR=PQPR = PQPR=PQ, so ∠RQP=180°−30°2=75°\angle RQP = \dfrac{180° - 30°}{2} = 75°∠RQP=2180°−30°​=75° → a).

  3. 3

    Part 3: S is on the major arc, so ∠RSQ=12∠ROQ=75°\angle RSQ = \dfrac{1}{2}\angle ROQ = 75°∠RSQ=21​∠ROQ=75° → b).

  4. 4

    Part 4: ∠ORP=90°\angle ORP = 90°∠ORP=90° (tangent ⟂ radius) → a).

  5. Check: in △PRQ, 30°+75°+75°=180°30° + 75° + 75° = 180°30°+75°+75°=180° ✔; in the kite ORPQ, 150°+30°+90°+90°=360°150° + 30° + 90° + 90° = 360°150°+30°+90°+90°=360° ✔.

  6. Answer

    1. c) 150° 2. a) 75° 3. b) 75° 4. a) 90°

    Common trap: Part 1: answering 30°, the angle at P. The angle at the centre is its supplement.

C2 — Case: the Sports Day logo (parts 1–3)●● StandardCase/source-based · 3 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Circles, Case Study 2 (parts 1–3)

(Picture, described: a white T-shirt printed with a triangle and a circle inside it touching all three sides.)

Varun has been selected by his School to design logo for Sports Day T-shirts for students and staff . The logo design is as given in the figure and he is working on the fonts and different colours according to the theme. In given figure, a circle with centre O is inscribed in a ΔABC, such that it touches the sides AB, BC and CA at points D, E and F respectively. The lengths of sides AB, BC and CA are 12 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm respectively.

  1. Find the length of AD

a) 7 b) 8 c) 5 d) 9

  1. Find the Length of BE

a) 8 b) 5 c) 2 d) 9

  1. Find the length of CF

a) 9 b) 5 c) 2 d) 3

(The bank's key: 1. a) 7, 2. b) 5, 3. d) 3 — correct. Parts 4 and 5 are left out: they say "If radius of the circle is 4cm" and ask for the areas of △OAB (keyed 24) and △ABC (keyed 60). A triangle with sides 12, 8 and 10 cm has area 157≈39.6915\sqrt{7} \approx 39.69157​≈39.69 cm² by Heron's formula, so its inscribed circle has radius 7≈2.65\sqrt{7} \approx 2.657​≈2.65 cm — a radius of 4 cm is impossible for this triangle.)

Full solution

Given: AB=12AB = 12AB=12, BC=8BC = 8BC=8, CA=10CA = 10CA=10 (cm). Asked: AD, BE, CF.

Concept used: piece at a corner =s−= s -=s− the opposite side (Topic 5). Why it applies: the sides are tangents.

  1. 1

    s=12+8+102=15s = \dfrac{12 + 8 + 10}{2} = 15s=212+8+10​=15 cm.

  2. 2

    Part 1: AD=s−BC=7AD = s - BC = 7AD=s−BC=7 cm → a).

  3. 3

    Part 2: BE=s−CA=5BE = s - CA = 5BE=s−CA=5 cm → b).

  4. 4

    Part 3: CF=s−AB=3CF = s - AB = 3CF=s−AB=3 cm → d).

  5. Check: AD+DB=7+5=12AD + DB = 7 + 5 = 12AD+DB=7+5=12 ✔, BE+EC=5+3=8BE + EC = 5 + 3 = 8BE+EC=5+3=8 ✔, CF+FA=3+7=10CF + FA = 3 + 7 = 10CF+FA=3+7=10 ✔.

  6. Answer

    1. a) 7 cm 2. b) 5 cm 3. d) 3 cm

    Common trap: AD=s−AB=3AD = s - AB = 3AD=s−AB=3 cm — the side to subtract is the one opposite A.
